agent_explanation: This pole fires at a word-onset token where the model is about to complete a familiar unit: subword fragments that begin a multi-token word (' tr' of 'trident', ' com' of 'com.intellij', ' The' of 'Thebes', 'Ren' of 'Renowned', ' Al' of 'Alcatraz') and determiners/possessives that open a stock phrase, above all the 'on the' / 'on their' frame ('on the move', 'on the market', 'on the table', 'on the rise', 'on their own'). It is not a plain token detector: ' the' reaches 6.3 in 'while they are on the' but 0.0 in a neutral sentence, ' tr' scores 3.7 after 'pulled the' where ' st'/' th' score 0.0/1.0, and the continuation fragment itself ('ident', '.intellij') is silent.

Fires at the seam where an element of an already-established repeated text format ends and the next slot of that format begins — the import slot after a Java package header, later entries of a JSON/INI/SQL/email-header/comment/diff/citation/table/numbered-list block — and, in prose, at the quote-close+attribution or the comma/dash that closes a long parenthetical insertion whose embedded clause has a lexical verb and its complement. The trigger is the structural boundary rather than the surface token: the same `import`, `,"`, comma or newline in free prose, as a lone or first occurrence, or after a short or verbless/copular quotation stays below threshold.

This pole fires on degree/comparison phrasing that qualifies how strongly a property holds: a degree modifier with a gradable head ('too'/'a little'/'a bit' + adjective, adverb or quantifier - 'a little too neat', 'a few too many', 'too much for them', 'too deeply ingrained'; adjectival 'enough'; the 'the X-er the Y-er' correlative), with the peak on the modifier, on its head, or - highest - on the function word that opens the phrase's complement ('to'/'be' in 'too long to be sent', 'for' in 'too neat for my taste', 'to' in 'general enough to treat'). It also fires on 'if' conditionals (peak on the following subject/copula, as in 'if something is ...'), on hedged modals ('seems like it ought to ...') and on the newswire byline 'Name (@handle)' at its closing parenthesis, whereas plain factual predication and bare intensifiers ('The book is neat', 'The book is very neat') leave it near zero.

Fires at a position where the model is partway into a proper name or word and must continue it with the next token, strongest (about 0.4 to 1.0 of max) when the continuation is a TV/radio broadcaster name, Japanese or US networks above all. Examples are ' T' before 'BS' in 'Fuji Television and TBS', 'テレビ' before 朝日/東京, '（' before テレビ in Japanese programme credits, ' and' in 'NBC, CBS, and' and ' i' in 'BBC iPlayer'. It is also strong on a lone word-initial letter piece of a tokenizer-split word, mostly p/P/T ('H+-p|umps', ' P|uts', ' p|acted', ' p|21'); complete words, standalone letters ('p < 0.05'), most other initial letters ('b|umps', ' H|ikes') and lists of non-broadcaster companies stay near zero.

Layer-0 lexical detector keyed on the current token's identity, with a small boost from the token just before it. It fires on a fixed set of whole words: ' Baseball'/' baseball', ' football', ' college'/' university', ' engineer(ing)', ' crane', ' army', ' soldier', ' surgeon', ' eye', ' ear', ' jumped'. Close neighbours outside the set stay low (' basketball', ' hockey', ' school', ' doctor', ' pilot', ' police', ' tree', ' arm', ' leg', single-token ' Josh'). It also fires on word-internal fragments ('osh', 'anth', 'ourn', 'ockey', 'oust', 'onaut', 'ene'), and these are much stronger when the previous token is the j-onset piece ' j'/' Jay' (j|osh, j|ockey, j|ournald, Jay|anthi) than when another onset precedes them (b|osh, t|ournald, r|ock|ey); a bare ' j' token gives only a weak ~0.27.

L15/N1604+ fires at boundary tokens inside a function/method call expression in code — the last fragment of a dotted callee (e.g. `click`, `autoDetectVcsMappings`), a comma between call arguments, or the `").`/`().`/`->` link that closes a call and continues a chain — and stays near zero on prose and on punctuation in standalone arrays and if-conditions. Its firing is set by the call-in-progress prefix (retrospective), while its output direction is tuned to the call's next element (`success`, `then`, `.each`, `.callback`, `(function`).

This neuron pole retrospectively detects lexical items denoting finiteness, discreteness, countability, or boundedness (such as 'finite', 'finiteness', 'discrete', 'countable', 'bounded', and 'limited') across mathematical, statistical, and general contexts. It activates maximally on explicit statements of finite cardinality or discreteness, shows moderate activation on antonymous bounds ('infinite', 'uncountable', 'unbounded'), and remains inactive on continuous, dense, smooth, or unbounded non-discrete concepts.

The pole fires on the token where the model is spelling out a word or formatted string it cannot resolve as a familiar English word: a first or internal piece of a foreign-language word or proper name, a rare or technical word, or an alphanumeric/reference string (DOI, citation key, CD marker such as CD62p, HTML attribute name, code/config/markup line). It is weak on complete common English words and plain English prose, and the same fragment fires much harder inside a non-English or formatted context ('Den kyske' vs 'the kyske', a full Gemfile vs a bare 's.license') than after an English function word ('the', 'and').

L6/N800- fires on a token that continues a multi-token unit opened by the preceding token rather than starting a new one: the later digit(s) of a multi-digit number ('4' in 94, '7' in 47, '0' in 350; never the first digit and not a one-digit number), a scale word after a numeral (' hundred' after One/Two/Three but not after 'Several' or 'A'), and non-initial pieces of multi-token words ('oral' in spatiotemporal, 'act' in biosurfactant, 'monary' in intrapulmonary, '_graph' in ..._graph_name). A weaker second component fires on abstract/technical content words (space, time, series, radius, sequential, dynamic, value, observations, measurements) when they sit in running expository prose, while the same words in other frames stay near zero ('a long time for the bus' 0.01, 'the space between the houses' 0.00, 'in sequential order' 0.01), so token identity alone does not explain when it fires.

The pole detects the stock 'more information / ask us / get in touch' formulae of written prose and peaks on their cue words: 'more'/'further' inside a purpose phrase ('For more information/details, ...' or '... for more details'), 'any' in 'if you have/need any ...', 'to' in 'do not hesitate to ...', and 'about'/'concerning'/'regarding'/'on' linking 'questions' to its topic. It does not fire on the bare directive itself ('Contact us', 'Visit our website', 'Click here'), on the same words in argument position ('she asked for more information', 'he did not hesitate to contact me'), or on ordinary conditionals ('if it rains'); because the peak is at the cue word, a fronted 'For more ...' is already active even when the continuation turns out not to be informational ('For more than twenty years').

N170+ is a personal-pronoun anaphora detector: it fires on a personal pronoun (I/my, you/your, he/him/his, she/her, we/our, they/them/their, or a reflexive like myself/himself/herself/themselves) when that pronoun agrees in person, number and gender with a person already mentioned in the preceding context, and it stays near zero on the very same pronoun token when the antecedent is absent (sentence-initial), only later (cataphoric), or gender/number-mismatched. The match is evaluated retrospectively against the recent context: repeated names and nouns never fire it, words after the pronoun do not change it, and a competing feminine mention nearby silences masculine pronouns while a salient feminine antecedent licenses she/her even alongside male mentions.

The pole fires on the token that completes an already-begun, low-frequency multi-token unit and thereby fixes its identity: the resolving fragment of a technical, code, maths or non-English word or identifier (prophyl|axis, CUMHURİ|Y|ETİ, AD|PK|D, BOOST_PP|_CAT, Abdelak|im, απ|ο|τελεί, the backslash of a LaTeX control sequence, base64 and macro continuations), the second word of a specialised compound ('partial', 'total', 'vapor', 'osmotic', 'systolic' + pressure), and the ' to' of the grammaticalised future 'going to'. It stays at baseline on the earlier fragments of the same unit (' proph', 'yl', 'İ', 'AD', 'BOOST_PP', 'Abdelak' all read ~0.0), on the same string when a space makes it open a word (' axis' 0.08-0.12 vs mid-word 'axis' 0.44-1.04), on ordinary English multi-token words (extraordinary, responsibility, internationalization), on everyday lexicalised compounds ('blood pressure' 0.09, 'magnetic field' 0.00), and on ' to' after any other verb or preposition ('walking to', 'went to', 'decided to', 'used to' all <=0.09 vs 'is going to' 0.90).

L4/N144+ is a retrospective 'specific-designator' detector: it peaks on the token itself when that token names a specific referent or technical construct — a proper name (Hillary, Chelsea, Saudi, Taliban, JetBrains), a numeral inside a date, citation or identifier (the 201x/202x year digits, 202-, 207450), or a technical/format token (://, //, [@, README, .hpp, print) — and stays near baseline on generic function words and generic nouns. Within that class it is selective and context-gated: long-tail or recent designators fire strongly in documents of the matching register (news, reference, code, medical, military), while high-frequency generic names (France, Google, Obama), older years (1998) and generic nouns (manual, show) stay near baseline, and the same word is much weaker in generic prose.

L3/N1429- is a token-level template matcher: it fires at the FINAL token of a small set of learned, low-frequency token templates (2-4 BPE tokens long) - technical identifier/API suffixes (',C URLOPT', '.find DOMNode', 'XML StreamReader', '* Factory', 'run_from _argv'), product/font names ('ES Xi', 'Solid Works', 'Semi Bold'), formal labels/names ('About the Publisher', 'World Economic History Congress', 'Hildebrant, Esq.', 'Israeli-Pale stinian', 'Jay anth') and fixed discourse phrases ('That, my', 'Hence, my') - and strength is graded by how much of the template prefix is present (VMware ESXi 2.31 vs ESXi 0.97; About the Publisher 1.34 vs the Publisher 0.04; Using SolidWorks 1.17 vs Using COSMOSWorks 0.12). It is a token-sequence match, not a word, compound, register or memorised-collocation detector: no token fires alone (all 151,936 single-token inputs <= 0.05); high-frequency collocations stay at baseline (New York, United States, Taylor Swift, Microsoft Windows, Joe Biden all <= 0.12); the same word in ordinary running prose stays at baseline (publisher, congress, search, works); the same surface words fail when the context tokenizes them differently (Bernie Sanders reaches 0.87 as Bern+ie+ĠSanders but 0.49-0.54 as ĠBernie+ĠSanders and 0.29 in prose); and changing one template token abolishes it (About the Publisher 1.34 vs About the Editor 0.04; World Economic History Congress 1.15 vs ...Conference 0.05).

The negative pole of L9/N758 fires on a content noun used as a kind or class term - typically the classifying first element of a multi-word term ('knee joint', 'climate change', 'competition authorities', 'Cancer Center', 'Bug Submitter', 'HTML5'), or a generic reference to the class in expository prose - with strength rising for specialist/technical, institutional or administrative vocabulary. It stays near zero on function words, on abstract relational nouns that take a complement rather than a compound head ('notion of', 'process of', 'agreement that'), on everyday nouns ('window', 'bicycle'), and on the same nouns used as particular instances in personal narrative ('his knee'); its output promotes no coherent token set (Jacobian kurtosis 3.3), so the pole is retrospective.

L22/N4106- is a computing/data-infrastructure term detector: activation is near zero on ordinary English prose but builds through passages that name computer hardware, network links and digital storage (Ethernet, USB, HDMI, SATA, WiFi, cable, wire, port, socket, plug, router, modem, motherboard, drive, RAID, filesystem, folder, file, database), peaking on the technical term itself or on the determiner/numeral/conjunction that introduces the next one (a, single, three, four, and), so the same function words fire inside a technical passage and stay silent in a garden, recipe or sports sentence with identical syntax. Non-English text and a few fixed specialised phrases (e.g. 'Police Act 1996', 'offensive tackle and guard') reach only about half the computing peaks, a weaker secondary offshoot rather than the main job.

The pole fires on the word that predicates a possession, attribute, or means of an entity or event: the verb HAVE (has/have/had, and cross-lingually French avoir 'a'/'avait') and the preposition WITH ('avec'), secondarily the obliques due/under, peaking on that word (often still elevated on the determiner that opens the complement). It does not fire on the copula (is/was/are), on structural prepositions (of/in/on/to), or where the same word is a lexicalised or comparative relator ('consistent with', 'compared with', 'a border with'), and its strength is set by the preceding frame: 'the theory / the compounds / an arrest ... has/have/with' is strong, while 'the room / the results ... has/have' and 'the man with ...' are weak.

The pole reads the onset of a Graeco-Latin word: it is strongest (about 17-21) on the bound word-piece that carries the Latin stem - ' mal'/' Mal', ' ben'/' bene'/' benef' - when the tokenizer splits it off the front of a longer word (malnutrition, maligned, malpractice, Benitez, benevolent), and it fires at 2-11 on whole word-initial tokens of the same learned stock (mathematical, medical, dental, linear, benign, malign, medicinal, molecular, neural). It is silent for ordinary, short or common words and for general academic vocabulary (normal, formal, hospital, benefit, biology, chemistry, analysis) and for the same letters buried inside one longer token (malaria, malfunction, Malta, mall), so it is neither an orthographic, a frequency nor a register detector.

Retrospective word-piece detector: the positive pole fires on a token that is a non-initial piece of a multi-token word — a token with no leading space that continues the orthographic word begun in the previous token — and peaks (~0.9-1.0) on the continuation piece, usually the first one, of an uncommon name, identifier or loan/technical word (C|orm|orant, J|op|lin, proper|Id, Ab|und|ant, eag|erness, Upps|ala, J|alan); the same string starting a fresh word after a space (property Id 0.39, property id 0.27) or a word-initial token fires far less, and word-specific rare fragments (Reykjavik's 'jav'/'ik', Kubernetes) do not fire at all. A second, distinct SwiGLU double-negative regime (gate<0 and up<0) fires on 'by' as the passive agent after a past participle (measured by, generated by), while every other 'by' variant is the pole's most-suppressed token in the vocabulary (negative pole = a 'by' detector); a weak whole-word component also fires on a few common words when they are the second element of a tight compound/collocation (student| pilot, right| now, to| have).

Retrospective grammatical agreement detector: fires in Romance languages (French, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian) on plural determiners, quantifiers, and pre-nominal or modifying adjectives (such as 'nouvelles', 'principales', 'las', 'das', 'des', 'as') agreeing with a feminine plural noun. It exhibits much weaker activation on masculine plural counterparts, and drops to near zero on singular forms and in non-agreeing languages like English.

Fires on the connective that hands a just-named plural category noun over to a list of its members: most reliably ', including' after a plural noun naming a class of entities (countries, cities, species, universities, artists, dishes; 0.4-1.0 of max, above threshold in >90% of 'several <class>, including' cases with ~500 tokens of prior text), and less reliably ', such as' / ', like' / ', notably' in the same slot (0.3-0.8, stronger in long documents, weak when there is no comma before them). It stays below 25% of max on 'including' that adds a component to an amount, price or duration ('the invoice/rent/fee, including tax', 'ten euros, including a drink', 'four hours, including stops', 'All costs, including tax'), after generic artifact categories (tools, instruments, materials), and on 'for example', 'for instance' and usually ', e.g.'; known leftovers predicted active are '<nationality adjective> state/province/canton of <Name>' ('the German state of Bavaria', not 'the state of Bavaria' or 'the city of Paris'), the WordPress footer 'This entry was posted ... and is filed under <Tag>', a clause-final ':' that opens an elaboration ('single-handedly: with ...', 'visible at once: the ...'; not reported speech 'He answered: ...'), LaTeX/code operators (' +', ' =', '\frac'), and a diffuse background (~0.6% of ordinary tokens reach 0.29-0.5) that makes most texts longer than ~150 tokens active, so only short texts without these triggers are predicted inactive.

This pole fires inside passages of genuine, verbatim boilerplate — software licence and copyright notices, CI/SSH console transcripts, and Stack Exchange 'A:' answer headers — peaking on the token that the fixed template makes nearly certain (e.g. ' established' after 'Connection' in an SSH transcript, ' KIND' in 'WITHOUT WARRANTIES OR CONDITIONS OF ANY KIND', ' changes' in 'Fetching changes...', the 'A' of an 'A:' header, 'c' of '(c)'). It does not respond to the same words in ordinary prose, to prose paraphrases of the same content, or to invented or truncated look-alikes of those templates, because the response builds over a preceding run of the real template rather than being carried by the word alone.

Retrospectively fires on tokens within spans describing the physical, anatomical, or structural features and components of biological organisms, cells, or mechanical implements. It remains inactive on abstract concepts, organizations, and figurative or non-structural descriptions sharing similar syntax.

The pole marks a definitional binding - a name or slot being tied to the content that fills it. In code it peaks on the ' =' (and still fires on ' :=') of a statement-level assignment binding an identifier to a value, and in prose on the modifier or head of a noun phrase whose referent is specified by a following complement ('a key component of...', 'a vital source of information', 'key factors that...', 'the only person that...'); the same words used without a binding - '==', '<=', '+=', keyword/default arguments, tuple unpacking, 'the key to the door', 'a vital issue', 'a source of water' - do not activate it.

Retrospectively fires on a qualifier that sits inside a phrase or relative clause restricting what a noun phrase picks out (or how far a claim holds): the negator of a reduced relative ('a service not listed', 'reactions not previously observed'), an epistemic or comparison adjective in a modifier ('variants of unknown significance', 'changes of unclear importance', 'with comparable/equivalent effects', 'with known effects'), a selective degree adverb ('particularly'/'especially', but not plain 'very'/'extremely'/'quite'), a partitive relative ('one of which'), and, in structured text, the value that fills a labelled slot ('Category:1903 births', a method's parameter list, an array-selector assignment). It is near zero on the same words used as a bare main-clause predicate ('the service is not listed', 'the changes have known effects', 'the subjects were particularly poor scorers') and on absolute magnitude or normality adjectives in the same slot ('beneficial', 'harmful', 'severe', 'major', 'typical', 'normal').

The negative pole fires on the vocabulary of conducting and analysing a quantitative study: extent adverbs that say how completely a manipulation or measurement was carried out when attached to study nouns ('study', 'experiment', 'trial', 'data', 'sample', 'specimens' - e.g. 'a completely randomized design', 'the specimens were randomly divided into three groups') and the names of study designs and statistical procedures ('repeated measures', 'two-way ANOVA', 'multivariate analyses', 'multiple/logistic regression', 'generalized linear mixed model', 'central composite rotatable design', 'three-stage sampling', 'prospective cohort', 'doubly robust', 'orthogonal' moment functions). The same surface words in ordinary narrative or about non-study subjects, and technical vocabulary that names objects rather than quantitative procedures, leave it at baseline ('The building was completely destroyed' 0.3, 'built randomly over the years' 0.0, 'the Krebs cycle'/'the Higgs boson'/'the Golgi apparatus' ~0), and the neuron's positive pole is silent on all of these inputs (<=0.04) while its write direction is the anti-'system' direction.
baseline_explanation: Fires on tokens related to "a person".

agent_explanation: The negative pole of L16/N1166 tracks a stated cardinality over discrete items of a made, copied or traded thing: it fires when the text says how many units/copies/instances of something exist, were built, made, printed, ordered, shipped or sold, how many remain, or what a single unit costs, peaking on the numeral, on unit nouns (copies, units, pair) or at the boundary where the counted phrase completes, and its output direction promotes quantity/count vocabulary (数量, 总数, number, quantity, copies, instances, batch). It stays near zero for measurement magnitudes (horsepower, percent, metres), dates, identifiers and count-free description, and the positive pole is near-silent on the scan corpus (max 0.93) while its lens suppresses those same quantity words; the lookahead gate is negative (KL 7e-3) so this is retrospective, even though per-position ablation shows the pole also nudges 'copies'/'made'/'produced' at count positions.

L1/N4067+ detects an out-of-vocabulary word being assembled: it fires on a word-internal subword fragment (a token with no leading space that is glued to the preceding piece of a multi-piece word) when the string is not an ordinary English word, e.g. 'ín' in 'Zemplín', 'a' in 'Mrdeža', 'ien' in 'økonomien', 'uka' in 'Otsuka', 'uba' in 'zubaan', 'View' in 'DataRowView'. It is near zero on word-initial pieces (the ' Z' of Zemplín, ' Mr' of Mrdeža), on whole common words, and on the ordinary morpheme continuations of common English words ('ization' in 'nationalization' scores 0.04), with only a much weaker tail (~0.2-0.4 of peak) on word-medial pieces of common English derivatives such as 'harden'.

L12/N40+ fires on a content word (usually the verb or the head noun of the relevant phrase) inside a clause that states how something is done or where something comes from, in instructional, methods, configuration or how-to text: 'reads the host list from a given file', 'filled from periodic data dumps', 'identified by conducting electronic searches', 'install the PSSH utility ... you can read this article', 'register with your social account or click here to log in', 'recruited by posting an advertisement'. The activation is graded and builds over about a sentence of matching context, and it is strongest when the means/source phrase names a concrete artifact (a file, variable, tool, data dump, menu, account, advertisement, article); it stays near zero on stative or definitional sentences that predicate a property of the same objects ('the cache is quite large and lives in memory', 'the host list is a file that the tool reads', 'the pscp tool is a utility for copying files'), on criteria lists, and on short general-narrative, news or legal sentences.

Retrospective detector of a program member/attribute name: the pole fires on the token that opens a name segment attached to a dot in source code (`config.timeout`, `obj.data`, `node.parent`, `buffer.index`, `rows.column`, `self.count`, `cache.size`), and more weakly on keys in structured literals (`"timeout": 30`, `height: 600`) and on `_`/camelCase segments of compound identifiers (`SSH_PRIVATE_KEY`, `rulesVisitor.ruleProperties`). It stays near zero on the same word used as an ordinary prose noun, on a bare local variable (`var count = n`), on keywords/operators, markup tags and quoted values, and it is lexically selective in the same `.member` frame: structural attribute names (`.data`, `.size`, `.count`, `.index`, `.parent`, `.column`, `.timeout`, `.state`, `.layout`, `.text`, `.items`, `.path`, `.file`, `.table`, `.node`, `.buffer`, `.rule`) fire, whereas common record-field names (`.email`, `.id`, `.user`, `.title`, `.address`, `.price`, `.date`, `.status`, `.code`, `.amount`) stay at zero; the scan's single strongest peak, the colon of a `Warning:` label in a PHP warning line, is an unexplained leftover.

The negative pole fires on the closing, dependent element of a two-part compound term: the classifying/relational adjective, participle or second component whose interpretation is supplied by the noun or prefix immediately before it (cell-specific, bacteria-positive, estrogen-dependent, sugar-free, fat-suppressed, pro-Israel, visual studio compatible, Meadow Brook, DumbAware, preintervention). It stays near zero on the same adjective when its left neighbour is an adverb or another adjective rather than a noun (very specific, quite based, small specific, very-positive) and on ordinary prose.

The pole fires on the linking or metalinguistic token that introduces a specific named expression: inside Title-Case (or quoted/italicised) work titles and name phrases it peaks on the lowercase connective (' of' in "The Picture of the Day", ' a' in "To Kill a Mockingbird", ' to' in "A Farewell to Arms", ' on' in "Attack on Titan"), and in term/label constructions it peaks on the word or field label that introduces the expression (' term', ' word', ' phrase', 'Terms like', 'Quote:', 'Keywords:', 'See also', 'abstract:'). The same words in ordinary lower-case prose, as isolated tokens, or in non-naming headings such as 'Notes:'/'Warning:' stay near zero, so the trigger is the name/term-mention frame rather than token identity.

Fires on the head noun of an indefinite noun phrase 'a/an (+ optional adjectives) NOUN' when that noun is an abstract, adverbial-idiom head (manner, way, fashion, basis, extent, level, minimum/maximum, glance, sense, attempt, while, time, rate, perspective, distance, hurry, whisper, percentage, degree; also 'friend'), as in 'in an efficient manner', 'on a daily basis', 'to a lesser extent', 'at a minimum', 'in an attempt'. The indefinite article is required: replacing 'a/an' with 'the', 'this', 'such a', 'my', 'no', 'any' or dropping it cuts activity to <=0.2 of max, and concrete nouns after 'a' (car, dog, house, table, room, project, idea, doctor) stay near 0; a preceding adjective (similar, lesser, timely, different) often fires moderately (0.4-0.6 of max) ahead of the noun.

Fires on the word 'official' used as an adjective or adverb meaning formally sanctioned or authorised status ('official trailer/website/figures/capacity', 'officially announced', 'now official'), and on its cognates in other languages (French officiel(lement), German offiziell, Spanish oficial(mente)), peaking on the token that completes the 'offic-' stem (e.g. 'iel', 'izi', 'ical'), at about 0.55-0.9 of max. It is much weaker (about 0.15-0.35 of max) for the noun sense 'a government official' / 'officials' and for near-synonyms 'unofficial', 'formally', 'formal', 'authorized'. It is essentially silent on 'office', 'officer', other status adjectives ('state', 'verified', 'personal', 'final'), and on the very first token of a text.

The positive pole fires on the first token of a singular, open-class classifier — a common count noun or a classifying adjective/noun adjunct, usually the first subword of a multi-token word — when it opens an indefinite (bare or quantifier-headed) noun phrase in running descriptive text: 'database drivers', 'hybrid vehicles', 'absorbent articles', 'statically-typed languages', 'shell scripts', 'cell phones'. It stays near zero when the same word is preceded by a definite/deictic determiner or 'a/an' ('the/these database drivers', 'an absorbent article'), when the word is itself plural-marked ('databases', 'drivers', 'cats'), and on proper names ('Toyota', 'China').
baseline_explanation: Fires on tokens related to "a type of writing".

agent_explanation: A detector for the bare word-initial piece "mal": it fires strongly (about 9-21 of max 18.5) whenever "mal"/"Mal" is tokenized as its own piece at the start of a word, with or without a leading space (' mal', ' Mal', and no-space 'mal'/'Mal' after a newline or quote) - malnutrition, maligned, malaise, malic, mal-adjusted, Maldives, Malawi, Malibu, Malfoy, Mal Turnbull, and the standalone French/Spanish/Portuguese word "mal" - in any context except the very first token of a text; secondarily it fires moderately (about 5-11) on the split-off pieces ' bene'/' ben'/' Beng' (benevolent, benediction, ben venuto, Bengali), on the name ' Ben' in most contexts (but not in the fixed phrases "Big Ben" or "Uncle Ben", about 0-2), and on ' mathematical' before a noun (about 7-14). It stays below threshold when the letters are fused into one longer token (malaria, malfunction, malware, malicious, malignant, malign, malt, mall, Malta, Mali, Malik, Malcolm, Mallory, benign, benefit, beneficial, bench, Benjamin, Bennett, Benson), on ' benef' in benefactor (2-5), on medical/medicinal/dental/linear (usually 1-5), and on all-caps MAL.

The negative pole detects the head of a clause-level circumstance adjunct from a small set — 'with', 'once' and the compound 'now that' — firing where that head is complete: on 'with' when it sits at a clause's left edge (sentence-initial after a full stop, newline or semicolon, or after a coordinator such as 'and'/'but' or the complementizer 'that'), on 'once' when it heads a clause (fronted or trailing, including sentence-initial idioms like 'Once again'), and on the 'that' of clause-initial 'now that'. The same words inside a clause are near zero — 'with' as a verb complement, NP-internal modifier, postposed or parenthetical with-phrase; 'once' as a clause-internal frequency adverb — as are other clause-initial prepositions and subordinators (in, at, by, for, after, when, if, because, although, while), which stay below the active threshold.

Fires on the first sub-word piece of a multi-token surname or place name: a short capitalised fragment, mostly W-initial (' We', ' Wo', ' Wa', ' W') and also ' Ra', ' Ke', ' Ka', ' Kl', 'ke', ' dela', that sits in a name slot (after a first name, a title such as Mr./Dr., or 'at'/'in' before an institution or place), so the word is still unfinished (Weisberg, Weill, Inverkeithing, Raanan). It stays silent on the same letters as a complete word (the pronoun 'We' at a clause start, single-token names such as Weber, Goldberg, Johnson, Inverness), on later pieces of the name ('ill', 'isberg'), and on other first pieces such as ' Gins', ' Br' or ' St'. A weaker offshoot fires on a pivot token inside memorised boilerplate, e.g. ' via' in a 'Sun-Sentinel via AP' photo credit and '=' in 'initial-scale=1'.

The negative pole responds to a field of a biology/medicine literature record, peaking on the separator or whitespace that opens its next field - the ':' in 'Magn Reson Med. 2019;81[:]2551-2565', the space before the pages when the same citation is written out as prose ('...in Magnetic Resonance in Medicine in 2019, volume 81, pages[ ]2551'), the space after '=' in an abstract's statistics ('95% CI =[ ]2.35-15.88'), and the ') (' that closes a long typed parameter list and opens the result list of a signature. Identically formatted citations carrying a physics/engineering/computing venue ('Phys Rev B. 2019;81:2551-2565', 'Adv Neural Inf Process Syst. 2017;30:5998-6008'), the same numbers in running prose, and ordinary narrative text stay near zero.

Fires on a transitive verb (or the perfect auxiliary 'have/has' right before it) whose direct object has already been supplied to its left, so no object is expected after it: the verb of an object-gap relative clause with or without 'that' ('the table I found', 'the house Jack built', 'the option people have had', 'everything you need'), or a participle whose subject is its patient ('a method has been developed', 'has been known'). It stays near zero on the same verb when an agentive subject precedes it and an object is still to come ('I found the table', 'engineers have developed a system', 'when it released the cables'); it reads only left context, and is strongest when the fronted head is an inanimate thing rather than a person.

The negative pole fires on the word-pieces of program identifiers (class, type, function, variable and package names) inside source code, peaking on the identifier's leading piece - ' Weather' in WeatherTodayModel, ' V'/'pn'/'Sites' in VpnSitesClient, ' aut' in autorest, ' graphics' in 'var graphics' - and staying elevated across the rest of the name, equally for declared and referenced names. It is near zero on language keywords, punctuation, operators, numbers and string text, and falls to roughly a tenth of peak when the very same words appear in ordinary prose (a code comment is intermediate); strength does vary between names (' Module', 'Sites', 'Sampling', 'Multi' fire several times harder than 'Client', 'Model', 'Foo'), which is the residual token-identity confound.

Fires on the token that commits a clause to putting forward something for others to accept or act on: the verb (its final subword) of demand/request/proposal/imposition verbs whose object is the content sought or proposed rather than a person (dictate, demand, request(ed), recommend, advocate, prescribe, propose, suggest, impose, submit, French 'ordonné'), the particle 'for' in 'asked/begged/called for', 'out' after verbs of calling out (yell/holler/call out), and 'Submitted:' in court-opinion headers; weaker (about a third to a half of max) on content-delivering verbs (mention, explain, clarify, contribute). It is near-silent on verbs of wanting or needing (want, need, require), deciding or handling (approve, reject, review, discuss, receive, get), giving (offer, provide, give), non-request 'for' (looked/waited/paid for), and person-object frames ('asked them', 'begged them', 'urged them'), which instead drive the negative pole; together the two poles split communicative verbs into 'acting on a person's mind' (negative) versus 'putting forward a demand or proposal' (positive).

L16/N4681+ fires on a non-initial piece of a multi-token word, name, number or identifier: the current token continues the previous token's word (it has no leading space), and its strength is highest on the fragment carrying the distinctive spelling of a rare/technical term (e.g. 'onal' in clonal, 'opt' in Hymenoptera, 'Instance' in m_pInstance, '.preventDefault', '9' in x509util). It is near zero when the same string begins a word after whitespace (' Instance' = 0.06 vs 'Instance' = 1.55) and on the split pieces of ordinary vocabulary ('ization' in institutionalization = 0.00), so it tracks word-internal continuation position rather than token identity alone.

Fires (retrospectively) on the token where someone's turn or response in an exchange is introduced or named: most strongly the opening quotation mark or colon that begins a quoted utterance right after a speech-act tag ("interrupted, “", "continued:", "interjected, “"), then reply/speech-act verbs in dialogue tags (answered, replied, insisted, suggested, asked, demanded; not non-speech tags like nodded, smiled, sighed) and nouns naming a chosen strategic response (move, switch, pick, choice, action, response, reply, counsel/defense), but not plain nouns like bill, plan, idea, trip or hire. A separate strong token-level offshoot: 'dominant' (and weaker 'recessive') as a mode of genetic inheritance ("autosomal dominant", "the gene is dominant"), plus 'no matter what'.

L15/N3118+ tracks a legal/regulatory framing of a transfer or holding of goods: it is active over the nominal naming the transaction (sale, selling, possession, distribution, trafficking, smuggling, transport, import, supply, manufacture, purchase, carrying) plus its linking function word, peaking on that word (' of'/' for'/' the') and returning to zero on the object NP; the object itself is irrelevant (knife, car, table, dog, person all give the identical 3.24). It is near zero when the same nominal is ordinary commerce with no legal frame ('the recent sale of a knife' 0.15, 'he was praised for the sale of a knife' 0.36) and for offences against persons in the identical 'charged with the X of' frame (murder 0.00, assault 0.00, robbery 0.00, theft 0.69), matching the scan peaks 'possession of heroin', 'distributing an image of a nude minor', 'the sale of counterfeit goods', 'illegal logging' and Dutch 'verkoop van' (sale of) under a ban.
baseline_explanation: Fires on tokens related to "political party".

agent_explanation: L14/N4442- fires on compact formal records - reporter/docket citations, party and counsel name lists, schema field labels, category tags, IDs and dates - and peaks on the delimiter that closes one field and opens the next (digits inside a citation number, a newline after a citation, a comma after a party name, ' of' in a field label, ':' after a field name). It is retrospective and value-blind: the word after the peak is irrelevant ('Place of Worship' and 'Place of work' both peak at 0.657; 'Colorado' and 'Montana' both at 0.474), whereas recasting the same content as a running narrative sentence costs 15-55% of the peak (category tags 0.56->0.30, medical fields 0.43->0.32, case citation 0.69->0.32); this is the weak lobe of a unit whose positive pole is a strong property-listing detector (listing copy drives the positive direction to 6.9) and whose output suppresses listing vocabulary (Jacobian lens: bedrooms, homes, condominium, residential, builder).

L23/N1769+ is a retrospective source-code name-slot unit: it fires at the position that opens an identifier in code - the colon before a type annotation ('let name' + ':' scores 8.4-9.7), a field or method modifier ('private' 8.6, 'public Notebook' 16.6), the generic bracket ('MutableMap<' 7.5), or the assignment before an expression ('n =' 13.0) - and at capitalised word pieces of such names in prose ('Brian', 'Paul', 'Outdoors'); among its high-activation positions the next token is capitalised in 43 of 57 cases against a 12% base rate. Its output substitutes the specific local name for the generic builtin: zero-ablating the pole restores +0.44 probability on 'Math' (JS 'n ='), +0.43 on 'String' (Java 'private List<...>'), +0.16 on '<String' (Kotlin 'MutableMap<') and raises 'List'/'Category'/'<K'/'n'/'parseInt' instead, and its strength is graded by the local type context - the same Swift ':' scores 9.7 where its struct declares 'let name: String' but 5.5 where it declares 'let name: Int', and the same Java constructor name scores 16.6 after a 'String' field but 12.0 after an 'Object' field.

Fires on a prefix (unary) operator token that opens an operand where the syntax expects an operand, not an operator, in code or arithmetic: above all a space-preceded unary minus ' -' right after a binary/comparison/logical operator, '=', ':=', ',', 'return' or a keyword ('5 - -3', '3 + -5', '&& -y', 'i == -1', 'foo(a, -1)', 'return -1'), strongest (~3-5.7) when the preceding token is itself an operator. Other operand-opening prefixes are weaker (unary ' +' ~2.5, ' ~'/' !' ~1-1.5, a regex-literal '/', an ObjC message ' [' in code), while the same ' -' used as a binary operator after an operand ('x - 1', '5 - 3', '3 - 2' in prose) and literals without a sign stay near zero.

Fires when the text has just stated that someone or something leaves, ends its tenure in, or is separated from a position, group, job, place or possession (leave, stepping down, left the, quit her, retired, forced out of, sold to, transfer from, until <year> after a held office, absence, will be lost). It peaks on the departure word or on the function word right after it, and stays near zero for the opposite (join, stepping up, entered, since, presence, saved) and for plain physical movement. A separate, weaker trigger is the colon after a language name in an etymology parenthetical such as '(Greek:' or '(French:'.

Fires on the first token that continues a sentence (mostly ',' but also ' (', ' -', ' and', ' however') right after a short, terse main clause that ends on a bare predicate whose complement is left implicit and recoverable from earlier context: VP ellipsis ('It did,', 'Martin doesn't,', 'You can,'), a bare adjective or intransitive verb ('It is possible,', 'They are still looking,', 'it was rarer,'), or a stranded preposition ('a model of,'). It is strongest when the clause is a curt answer to or comment on a topic set up well before (e.g. 'It is possible,' answering a 'Can I...?' question), weak when the clause carries an explicit object or complement ('You can subclass FileInputFormat,'), and near-silent on semicolons, on commas after introductory adverbials ('Yes,', 'In the winter,') and on list commas; leftovers include decimal and thousands separators after a number that could have ended the clause ('$9[.]38', '300[,]000').

L2/N3729+ is a retrospective two-token 'completion' detector: it fires at a position whose token does not start a word but finishes a unit that the previous token(s) already began, and is near zero at the first token of that same unit. The units are (i) words split over BPE pieces (' j'+'ourn' 3.96, ' J'+'.' 3.0, 'fire'+'h'+'ose' 0.9, 'XML'+'Input'+'Factory', ' journal'+'ing'), (ii) dotted or hyphenated technical names ('java'+'Script', 'java'+'.net', 'jquery'+'-'+'3'), and (iii) the second word of a bound two-token name or phrase ('Rio'+' Grande' 1.6, 'Jackie'+' Chan' 1.5, 'Jake'+' Jones' 0.6, 'Task'+' Force' 0.8, 'Today'+''s' 1.2, 'Justice'+' of' 2.3, 'should'+' he' 1.1). What matters is the pair, not either token: the first token of the unit is flat (' J' 0.47, 'Rio' 0.02, 'Justice' 0.15, 'should' 0.09), and swapping only the completing token for a same-slot alternative collapses the pole ('J.' 3.0 vs 'M.' 0.15; 'Rio Grande' 1.6 vs 'Rio Bravo' 0.0; 'Jackie Chan' 1.5 vs 'Jackie Brown' 0.0); frequent but weakly bound pairs are residuals the claim does not cover ('New York' 0.01, 'John Smith' 0.0).

Fires on the opening tokens of a conjunct that follows a bare comma (or a line break) with no conjunction, i.e. the second or later member of an asyndetic list or parallel series ("dimers, trim[ers]", "word processor, office [suite]", "easier to read, [more]", "six physicians, [six]", "1. ..., [2].", comma-spliced parallel clauses "shape, responses [were]"). It peaks on the token that completes the new conjunct's head (often the second token after the comma). It stays near zero when the conjunct is introduced by 'and'/'or', a semicolon or a full stop, and after non-coordinating commas (introductory adverbials, subordinate clauses, appositives, vocatives); single-token items in plain noun lists fire only weakly.

N3907+ is an exact-form name detector: it fires on a token that belongs to a canonical, verbatim technical name or reference string that must be reproduced as-is - a proper technical name ('Soft Matter' 2.3-3.5 on ' Matter'; 'Macromolecules' 2.22), a bibliographic or legal reference formula ('ASBCA Nos.' 2.08; 'Korean Application No.' 1.44 on ' No'; 'vol. 338, no. 6109' 1.48), a fully-qualified code name ('javax.ws.rs.ext.Provider' 1.41 on '.Provider'; 'Gem::Specification' 0.80) or a multi-part identifier. It is near zero when the same token carries ordinary vocabulary or a paraphrase of the string - ' Matter' after ' Water' 0.10, 'soft matter' 0.10, lowercase 'macromolecules' 0.00, 'Application Number' 0.48, 'Nos' without its period 0.38 - and invented or placeholder identifiers do not fire either ('com.example.Provider' 0.03, 'Journal of Zorblax Studies 12:34-56, 2020' 0.36), so the pole tracks attested name strings, not identifier syntax or capitalisation in general.

Fires on the first piece of a word the tokenizer has split, a short fragment that is not a word by itself and must be continued by a suffix piece. It is strongest when that fragment is a lone r/R or w/W (also U), especially right after a hyphen or slash ('re-r|outed', 'most-w|atched', 'nerve-r|acking', ' R|OLLBACK', ' UR|GENCY', ' r|ica', 'men/w|omen'), and also fires on short non-word stems such as ' rep|umping', ' typ|ologically', ' sw|ivel', ' Str|asbourg'. It is near zero on complete single-token words (' top', ' rebooting', ' ENERGY'), on the continuation pieces themselves, on fragments starting with most other letters (' p|obre', '-h|ated', '-s|orted', ' H|ORIZONS'), and is weaker when the same word already appeared earlier in the text. Unlike the positive pole, which fires partway into broadcaster and other proper names, this pole tracks the opening fragment of an unfinished common word. A secondary case is ' Best' opening an award category ('nominated for Best Picture').

Fires on the OPENING delimiter of an inline markup span in prose or scientific text, i.e. the token that starts a Markdown/Pandoc formatted run glued to the following word: Pandoc subscript/superscript '~' and '^' (as in T~2~, (SurfO)~2~, 2^nd^), Markdown emphasis ' *' / ' _', fused italic tokens like '_N', '_O', '_the', and Apex '__' in '__c'; the matching closing delimiter stays near zero, the same characters used as ordinary punctuation or code identifiers (my_var, H_2O, -, =) do not fire, and activation is much stronger when the document has already used that kind of inline markup earlier (the second '~'/'^'/'_' opener beats the first, and bare ' _' italics barely fire without prior markup). Weaker leftovers (~0.3 of max) are other span-opening punctuation such as opening quotes, parenthetical dashes ' –', ' /' in '/CNW/' and a dateline comma.

N2268- fires on the second token of a two-token unit that the preceding token has already committed to: a particle or preposition after an event/action word ('go about' 2.4, 'go over' 1.4, 'go around' 1.3, 'set up' 1.0, 'ready up' 1.1, 'plan up' 0.9, 'look about' 0.8), or the tail fragment of a word continued across two tokens ('Ke|isha' 1.1, 'Comp|iling' 0.7, 'Ans|ar' 0.6). Both tokens are required: the same particle after a determiner, pronoun or concrete noun is silent ('the up', 'hands up', 'table up', 'the word about' all ~0), the same verb with a particle outside the preferred set is near silent ('go back' 0.00, 'set out' 0.00, 'set aside' 0.00), and a non-event verb roughly quarters it ('put up' 0.37 vs 'set up' 1.16).

Layer-0 subword bigram detector: fires on a word-internal continuation token (no leading space) such as 'ley', 'PE', 'uk', 'RA', 'w', 'rie', 'ry', 'pose', 'aler', 'ale', 'rah', 'to', 'TE', '4' when the immediately preceding token is a short word-start fragment ending in P/p or h/H (' P', 'P', ' Ch', 'ch', ' Sch', ' H', ' Ph', ' Sh', ' AP', ' MP', ' EP', 'Sup', ' Rip', ' Ash'); it stays near zero when the same continuation follows any other fragment or whole word (' K'+'rie', ' Kings'+'ley', ' Prop'+'ose', 'Q'+'450'), when the continuation carries a leading space (' P'+' w'), on the prefix token itself, and on continuations outside the set ('ola', 'ina', 'ett', 'ford'), independent of wider context.

N3252- is a layer-0 detector for the subword pieces that spell chemical-structure morphemes: it fires on tokens such as 'yl', 'ethyl', ' methyl', 'ene'/'ylene', 'ane', 'ox'/'xy', ' hydro', 'amine', 'ide' and the acid/salt pieces (' acid', ' phosphate', ' chloride'), reaching 1.2-5.1, while chemistry topic words that arrive as a single token stay near zero ('epoxy' 0.20, 'dioxide' 0.00, 'peptide' 0.00, 'protein' 0.02, 'steroid' 0.11) and words that merely contain the same letters do not fire ('style' 0.05, 'Kyle' 0.00, 'phylum' 0.00). The piece's own spelling sets the level and is essentially position- and right-context-invariant ('phenyl' gives 5.07/5.17/5.20 at three positions and 5.065/5.065/5.073 before three different following words), while the preceding piece modulates it (same 'yl' piece: 5.07 after ' phen', 4.36 after 'hen', 1.27 after 'proph').

Fires on an opening or boundary token after which a fresh word will start with no leading space: strongest (10-12) when such a non-word token is the very first token of the text ('[', '
', '

', '---
', '{
', '"'), and moderately (3-10) mid-text on a line or paragraph break that ends a title, question or label (':

', '?

', '.
') or on an opening ' (' / ' [' / ' "' that starts a parenthetical or quote. It is near zero on word tokens, including a first token that is a word ('The', 'So'), and on any token followed by a space-prefixed word (e.g. ',' or ' ' in place of the break). Its output promotes spaceless word-start fragments ('sc', 'sm', 'g', 'gl') as a broad class, not specific tokens.

Fires on a token whose text begins with the letter sequence 'str' (any case, with or without a leading space or hyphen), strongest (about 0.5-1.0 of max) when that token is a bare sub-word fragment such as 'str', ' Str', 'Str', '-str', ' strat', ' stre' that opens a longer word or name (stratospheric, Stringer, Stroud, Lindström, strait, single-stranded, stratification); whole-word 'str' tokens are weaker (' string', ' strategic', ' strict', ' stretch' about 0.1-0.6, depending on context), very common whole words (' strong', ' street', ' structure') are near zero, and tokens without the 'str' onset (' St', 'thr', ' D') are inactive. It is retrospective: the activation reads the current token's spelling, with little dependence on earlier context, and the Jacobian lens (kurtosis 3.2) promotes no coherent next-token set.

N546+ is a long-range discourse-topic detector: it fires on a content word (noun or verb) whose meaning fits the topic established by the preceding passage, and its strength grows with how much topical context has accumulated (the word 'debt' in a finance passage reads 0.01 with no context, then 0.15 / 0.20 / 0.30 after 1 / 2 / 3 finance sentences). The same word in an unrelated passage falls to ~0, a related word that was never mentioned (loan, borrowing) still fires (~0.29), and function words, formulaic or idiomatic content words and locally well-formed but off-topic words stay near zero, so the trigger is semantic topical fit with the long context, not the token's identity, frequency or local predictability.

Layer-0 lexical detector: fires on the current token itself (about 70-95% of the drive; the preceding token adds at most ~0.15 of max) when it is one of a fixed set of word-forms, strongest (>=0.7 of max) for history/History, approach, work/Working, Architecture, problems, args, a closing brace '}', and Chinese 工作/这样做/历史, medium (0.3-0.6) for process, research, interface, probably, problem, arguments, running, type, function, and weak (<0.3) for modal/hedge words such as would/could/usually. It is not a concept detector: close synonyms that are different tokens (heritage, tradition, tackle, method, procedure, labor, issues, params, Platform) stay near zero, and the words around a trigger barely change its activation.

The negative pole of L13/N2052 is a Wikipedia category-markup detector: it fires when the text contains a wiki category declaration ('Category:<term>', and even more strongly '[[Category:<term>]]'), ramping through 'Category' and ':' to a peak on the opening tokens of the category term, and it fires hardest when that term begins with a 4-digit year ('Category:1903 births/films', peak ~2.0 locally and 3.4 in full articles), less for word terms ('Category:Italian cyclists' ~1.4) and single words ('Category:Physics' ~0.9). The trigger is the wiki category syntax plus a year-like value, not the tokens or the year itself: running prose ('He was born in 1903', 0.2), ordinary label lines ('Name: John Smith' 0.07, 'Year: 1903 births' 0.46), CSV rows and infobox fields stay near zero, and a minority of strong activations (5 of the 20 scan examples, in non-wiki prose) are not explained by this hypothesis.

Fires on the first token of a quoted or cited utterance that the narration presents as a sample of what someone says or answers: the opening quote mark or first word after 'saying things/words/phrases like' or 'such as' (strongest), and the leading reply word ('Yes', 'Yeah', 'Oh', 'Sure') right after 'replied/answered/said, "'. Its second, related job is the all-caps license-file name (' LICENSE', ' COPYING', ' NOTICE') when the text points the reader to that file ('See the ___', 'found in the ___ file'). A bare quote after 'said' or 'the word', lower-case 'license', and other file names such as README or AUTHORS stay near zero.

The negative pole fires on a personal pronoun (you, I, we, she, he, they; weaker for me/your/her and for 'one'/'someone') that opens the subject slot of a new, usually subordinate or embedded clause right after a linking word (when, if, in case, should, so, hoping, help, let, sparing, what), whose referent is NOT an earlier-mentioned person: deictic or generic 'you/I/we', or a hypothetical 'she/he/they' in text about objects or advice. It is the contrast to the positive pole (pronouns that refer back): it drops sharply when a third-person pronoun has a matching earlier human antecedent ('The nurse ... when she'), and stays near zero on 'it', on names and full noun phrases in the same slot, on sentence-initial main-clause pronouns, and on non-pronoun words, while deictic 'you' is unaffected by an earlier person.

In prose that reports experimental or debugging results, fires on the last token of a clause's subject (head noun, closing ',' or ')' of an appositive or relative clause, or a pre-verbal 'also'/'it'), when that subject names a manipulation, agent or tested condition (gene knock-out, drug treatment, inhibitor, oligomers, 'when I comment it out') and the predicate about to follow will report its observed effect. It is strongest when a negative or contrastive outcome is set up ('None of the ...', 'however', '... did not'), and weak or absent when the same noun is an object or a procedural or descriptive mention ('we stored the oligomers', 'read-out of the gene') or appears in non-experimental narrative.

Fires on a sub-word token that ends exactly at a Greek/Latin combining-form prefix, linking vowel included, when the token is a bare prefix waiting for its stem or used on its own: 'micro'/' micro'/' Micro' strongest (~0.8-1.0 of max, e.g. ' micro|flora', 'micro|seconds', 'a new micro'), then 'tetra' ('tet|ra'), 'angio' ('ang|io'), 'icosa' ('icos|ah'), 'andro' ('And|ro'), 'xylo' ('xy|lo'), 'polyc', ' macro' (~0.5-0.9), and weaker for ' nano', ' mega', ' mono', ' poly', ' multi', ' mill', ' hex', ' hydro' (~0.25-0.5). It stays near zero on whole-word tokens that only contain such a prefix (' microwave', ' microscopic', ' microtime', ' nanoparticles', ' psychology'), on fragments cut before the linking vowel (' angi', ' cy', ' tri', ' di'), on ordinary words, and at the first token of a sequence. The context before the token barely matters.

Fires on a word naming a field of artistic, aesthetic or vernacular culture: design, art, folklore/folk, popular (as in popular culture or vote), costume, opera, sculptor, singers. It fires hardest when the word labels the whole discipline or category ('Cover design by', 'design has become', 'popular culture', 'In folklore') rather than a concrete object, and stays near zero for the same frames filled with non-cultural domains (finance, tax, medicine, price, chemistry, code). Retrospective: the peak is on the culture word itself and is driven mostly by that token and its immediate modifier.

Fires on a segment token (usually starting with '.', '/', '-' or a version digit) two or more segments into a URL, namespace URI or dotted/slashed import path when the segments before it spell a familiar, often-copied boilerplate string, so the segment completes a memorized canonical path: schemas.android[.com], msdn.microsoft.com/en[-us], code.jquery.com[/jquery], github.com/Azure[/go], android.support.v[7], django[.db], org.apache.commons.net[.]. Replacing an earlier segment with an unfamiliar name (example, zorblat, x9) mostly removes it, generic URLs and file paths (www.google.com/search, C:\Users\..., com.example.myapp) and ordinary prose stay near zero, and memorized prose or message boilerplate ('error: no known class method', traceback 'line 10,') gives only weak to moderate activity.

Fires on the word that opens an argument slot (a preposition such as to/on/for/of/at, the conjunction 'or', or a transitive operation verb such as maps/lists/click/attach) in technical, computing or scientific text when that slot is about to be filled by an inanimate technical entity (a file, directory, UI element, key, cable, query, feature or stimulus), e.g. 'No such file [or] directory', 'right click [on]', 'skipping queries [for]', 'Visual attention [to] features', 'The config file [maps]'. It stays near zero when the same frame expects a person as filler (explain/hand/introduce X to, talked to, popular with, 'No such person or') or on content nouns themselves; consistent with this, its output suppresses person nouns (' people', ' users', ' developers', ' students').

Retrospective detector of literal, vivid descriptions of physical scenes and bodies in motion. It fires on the concrete noun, or on the 'nearly/almost' + motion verb, when a natural object or body part does something physical: strongest on the literal word 'sun' (the sun came up/rose/set), then on things like branches pushing through a roof, eyebrows/heart 'nearly' touching or stopping, an eagle's wings 'and soared', waves 'crashed' on rocks, leaves 'rustled', and on 'fast' in the stock phrase 'X is fast approaching'. It stays near zero for the same words in non-physical, figurative or institutional use ('the band came up', 'Sun Microsystems', 'over the moon', 'raining cats and dogs', 'moving fast.', 'nearly finished the report') and on technical or administrative text; sporadic peaks on mid-word subword pieces of rare words (capecit|ab|ine, Gurt|ov|oy, Danish ' ø|konomien') are leftovers that this hypothesis does not predict.

The pole fires at a clause's left edge on a fronted adverbial prepositional or negative phrase from a small opener set ('In', 'On', 'At', 'For', 'Upon', 'Not', 'Unless'), peaking on the opener itself, or on the ' the' that immediately follows 'On'/'At'/'In', when that phrase opens a sentence (after '.', '.\n\n', ':' or a line break) or opens a clause after a coordinator ('And in 1999', 'But on Thursday', 'on the other hand' after 'but'/'that'). The same preposition placed later in the clause - postposed, appositive or a verb complement ('opened a factory in 1999', 'reported results on Thursday', 'put his hat on the bench') - stays near zero, as do fronted openers outside the set ('When', 'After', 'Before', 'By', 'During', 'Under', 'Since', 'Through', 'From', 'With', 'Once'); weaker residual peaks on fixed collocations ('prime minister', 'sat on', 'the most significant') are not explained by this.

Fires on verse/lyric material and, separately, on fixed alphanumeric literals. It peaks on the vocabulary of verse ('lyrics', 'lyric', 'poem', 'sonnet'), on the surname that completes a poet's or songwriter's full name ('Robert Frost', 'Emily Dickinson', 'Bob Dylan'), on the colon-plus-newline that introduces a quoted verse line after such a word ('the second verse:

', 'Here are the lyrics:

'), and on a digest inside an HTML integrity attribute ('sha384'/'sha512') or a LaTeX exponent/limit term ('$x^2+y^2=1$', '$\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-1}$'). It stays near zero for prose fiction and novelists ('the complete novels of Charles Dickens', 'John Steinbeck'), for the abstract words 'poetry'/'poet', for quoted prose, for numbers, dates and version strings in running prose, for arbitrary hash-like strings that are not a recognized digest or formula, and for the same 'sha384' string when it appears in prose instead of an attribute; individual poet names vary (Keats, Shakespeare and Milton do not fire).

Fires on words that denote the authorities taking a person into restraint, i.e. arrest, detention, custody or jail ('arrested', 'under arrest', 'into custody', 'detention'/'détention', 'sent to jail', 'caught'/'apprehended' by police, 'imprisoned'), on the illegality marker 'Unlawful/unlawful', and on the preposition right after such a verb ('arrested for', 'jailed for', 'imprisoned for'). It is weak or silent when the same word has a non-criminal sense ('joint custody', 'the ball was caught', 'in this case', 'a case of beer') and on conviction or sentencing words ('convicted', 'sentenced to', 'prison' all stay below 0.1 of max). It is retrospective: the Jacobian lens suppresses criminal/sentencing tokens rather than promoting the next token.

Layer-0 single-token (unigram) detector for a fixed, semantically unrelated lexicon: it fires on the current token alone when that token is one of a specific set, strongest on 'monary' (the tail of cardiopulmonary/extrapulmonary, ~1.0), 'Classic' (no leading space), 'Jean', ' favorite'/' favourite', 'la' (S-la-ughters), 'StringRef', 'ties' (Six-ties), 'yth' (Fors-yth), 'au' (Nass-au), 'egade', ' NEGLIGENCE', ' steady', ' pulmonary', ' console', ' mening', 'oph' (es-oph-agitis), ' Manhattan', ' BOOST', and stays near zero on close synonyms or same-domain neighbours ('Modern', ' passion', ' stable', ' terminal', ' renal', ' hepatitis', ' gastr', 'Jan' only ~0.3). Surrounding context barely matters (the preceding token shifts strength by at most ~0.1-0.3 of max, e.g. ' JS' before 'StringRef' raises it), so the same trigger token fires in any sentence, register or language.

A layer-1 spelling-fragment detector: the negative pole fires when the current token is one of a learned set of unusual letter fragments that occur as non-final pieces of names, acronyms and technical or foreign words - 'US' after 'V' (VUS), 'PT' after 'F' (FPTCs), 'MT' after 'E' (EMT), 'OP' after 'C' (COPD), 'AY' after 'H' (HAYNE), 'orm' after 'c' (cormorant), 'ank' after 'K' (Kankakee), 'uv' after 'ma' (mauvaises), 'æ' after 'hj' (hjælpe) - and on the name-onset tokens ' Hay'/'Hay' (Hayne, Hayao), ' Tay' (Tayyip), ' Bog' (Bogut) and ' Anderson', plus a smaller glue family of hyphen pieces ('-free' after 'risk'/'gun', '-engine' after 'reverse', '-' in 'X-Plane', the minus in '3*a - 7'). The trigger is the specific fragment, not the word's rarity or meaning: equally rare names and technical words with ordinary spellings (Kowalski, Nakamura, apoptosis, cholangitis), the same letters inside common words (bay, dorm, bank, corner, corn, GTP, 'haystack' as a single token) and ordinary prose all stay near zero, while the positive pole of the same SwiGLU unit fires on a disjoint fragment set ('ao' in Hayao, 'ot' in luaotfload).

Fires on website cookie/tracking-consent notice boilerplate, i.e. a site telling its visitor that it uses cookies (or analytics/tracking) to give them the best experience and that continuing to browse/use the site means they agree (English, French and other languages). Activity builds across the notice clause and peaks on the sentence-ending punctuation (or the following 'By'/'This') right after a 'we use cookies to ... experience/website' or 'this site uses cookies' clause; it is near zero when cookies are a topic rather than a notice (browser cookie how-tos, studies about cookie banners) or food (bake/eat cookies, jar of cookies), and weak (~0.15-0.45 of max) on adjacent legal boilerplate like reCAPTCHA notices, newsletter sign-up privacy lines and GPL licence headers.

Fires on a hedge or approximator word at the moment it marks the following quantity, amount or claim as inexact or non-absolute: numeric approximators ('about'/'around'/'roughly'/'approximately'/'nearly'/'almost' before a number, '... or so'), vague plural quantifiers in a quantity slot ('for many years', 'several hours', 'worth much more', 'three to six'), and epistemic or extent hedges on a predicate ('probably', 'maybe', 'perhaps', 'mostly', 'largely', 'hardly', 'generally'). It stays near zero for the same words in non-hedging senses (topical 'talked about', spatial 'walked around'), for precise or boundary qualifiers ('exactly', 'only', 'even', 'certainly', 'or more'), for bare numbers, and for plain intensifiers or pre-verbal frequency adverbs ('very', 'often', 'usually'); activation sits on the hedge token and does not depend on what follows it.

The pole fires on the word that asserts positive instrumental value, importance or necessity: an evaluative predicate of a copular value claim ('the marker is helpful / useful / important / essential / critical / crucial / effective / beneficial for|in X', incl. 'instrumental', 'vital', 'invaluable'), or a contribution noun heading such a function claim ('plays a role / has a part in', 'the importance of', 'has the capability to', 'holds promise for'). It stays near zero when the same adjective merely modifies a following noun ('a useful tool', 'an important finding'), when a value-irrelevant or harm/severity adjective fills the same predicate slot ('large', 'fast', 'beautiful', 'delicious', 'harmful', 'severe', 'toxic', 'rare'), and when a role is only mentioned or denied ('the role was reversed', 'suggest a role for') rather than asserted.

Detects the orthographic stem "deci-" in any language or casing, mainly the decide/decision family (decide, decided, deciding, decision(s), decisive, undecided, indecisive, decidir/decisión, décidé/décision, decisões) plus offshoots that share the letters (decimal, deciliter, decibel, deciduous). It fires on the token that completes the stem, and fires hardest when the stem is split across tokens (Dec+ided, Dec+ide, DEC+ISION, DEC+IMAL, inde+cis, decis+ões; roughly 5-9) rather than held in one whole-word token (' decided', ' decision', ' decimal'; roughly 1.5-4). It stays near zero on other "dec-" words (deceive, decorate, December, declare, decree only ~0.9), on look-alikes (divide, division, divisive, precise, concise) and on synonyms (choose, choice, resolved, agreed).

Retrospective: fires on a whole content word (noun, adjective, gerund, adverb, a sentence- or line-opening word, or the last piece that completes a tokenizer-split title word such as Cer|emony, Butter|flies, Sur|prising) whose identity the PRECEDING words did not predict, most strongly for abstract, institutional, collective or quantity/size words (knowledge, support, record, history, evidence, army, government, world, market, training, number, large, small) sitting right after an article, preposition, possessive or a sentence/line start; whether the word fits what comes after is irrelevant, so 'A large number of...', 'The world watched', 'the training program', 'after years of wrestling' and 'caused by number of' are all active. It stays near zero when the left context nearly forces the word ('for all of your support', 'Second World War', 'world record', 'basic training', 'stock market', 'in the history of'), on function words, pronouns, digits, punctuation, code keywords and the very first token of a text, and is usually weak (under ~0.3 of max) on a noun that follows an adjective and on mundane concrete nouns (chair, dog, car, park, shop, shirt, snow) even when they are surprising.

The negative pole fires where a text picks out a specific, individually identifiable item as the target of a pointing or relational phrase, peaking on the label/name token itself: numbered or labelled items of the current task ('from problem 6', 'see question 6', 'after completing Step 1', 'according to Table 9', 'from comment #0'), named entities that belong to the passage's own subject matter ('Cannon Falls' in a place article, 'Reiner Torres' in a canoeist biography, 'the 1956 film PraiKuarng'), and the identity/comparison/pointer constructions that introduce them ('the same as X', 'a sequel to X', 'together with X', 'more X than Y', 'See X', 'href=', 'REFERENCES'), with the activation decaying over the rest of the reference. It is much weaker for a bare definite or indefinite description in the same slot ('from the problem' 0.40 and 'from a problem' 0.33, 'see the question' 0.46, as fractions of the scan scale, against 0.8-1.2 for the numbered label), near zero (0.02-0.25 of scale) for pronouns and for nouns or proper names outside the passage's domain ('see it', 'see him', 'see the boat', 'from Boston', 'together with a teammate'), for a labelled item that has just been mentioned in the same passage, and in plain description or narration with no such referent.

The pole fires on four specific slots, peaking on that token: (1) the preposition that introduces the weapon or instrument in a scene of violence or crime, set by the scene rather than the verb ('attacked his wife with a screwdriver', 'the gunman met the guard with a rifle', also 'using', and cross-lingually only here: French 'avec' and Spanish 'con' in 'atacó ... con un cuchillo'; about 2.5-4); (2) attributive 'due' and the degree adjective of a manner 'with' phrase ('due process/diligence/respect', 'with great care/confidence', including sentence-initial 'With great care,'; about 2.4-4.7, while clause-final 'due to' is weaker at about 1.1-1.6); (3) a year digit, usually the last, in copyright notices and parenthesised birth-death dates ('Copyright (c) 2016', '(5 July 1914 - 11 April 2009)'; about 1.4-3.1); and (4) more weakly (about 1.0-2.3), has/have right after a chemical, drug, molecule or theory subject that states its property or effect ('the drug has no effect', 'the compound has a melting point'). It is inactive (below about 0.9) on years in running prose ('built in 1940', 'In July 1914'), predicative 'is due', non-violent tool use and comitative, noun-modifying or lexicalised with/avec ('fixed the shelf with', 'helped his wife with', 'the girl with the red hat', 'agree with', 'diagnosed with', 'La chambre avec balcon'), sentence-initial possessive 'With three assistants...', possession HAVE with an ordinary subject (person, organisation, place or building: 'the hotel/museum/committee has', French 'Le musee a une collection', 'I/we/you have'), and modal 'have to', where 'have' and 'to' stay below 0.5 (the one known leftover is 'Visitors have to show a badge', at 1.4 on 'show').

Fires on the words of a passage that names the medical treatments, procedures or devices given to a patient (lists of therapies, drugs, catheters and interventions). It peaks on the list connectors (',', ' and', ' of', ' using', ' with') and on the sub-word pieces of the treatment terms inside that span (e.g. 'drug therapy, insertion of an implantable', 'intr|avenous', 'permanent vascular access'). The same words in a non-medical frame (holiday options, a guest, a garden hose, a varnished table), or in a list of symptoms, stay weak or near zero. A smaller set of peaks comes from non-English or code sub-word fragments (' ten'|'aient', 'document'|'atie', ' m'|'uffs', 'navbar'), which are token-specific leftovers.

The pole fires on the first token of the word that continues a specific, individuated noun phrase: the head of a name-noun or technical noun-noun compound ('Hawaii residents' 1.27, 'company chief' 1.25, 'stent lumens' 2.14, 'CAMC's core' 2.52) or the copula/preposition that opens that noun's predicate ('this tune is' 2.05, 'the report of the committee was' 0.55, 'the game with' 1.97). It stays near zero when the same slot holds a generic qualifier ('local residents' 0.00, 'Nearby residents' 0.19, 'CAMC's good values' 0.32) or a clause-opening relativizer/coordinator ('the report that the committee...' 0.10, 'Hawaii and residents' 0.16), so neither the trigger-token list nor 'fires after any noun' predicts it.

The pole fires on a preposition (mostly ' at' or ' on', also ' for', ' as' (and the article after it), ' under', ' by') that opens a second, different-role adjunct of the clause directly after a finished PP of place, population or audience whose object is a closed referent: a 'City, Region' name pair ('He died in Portland, Oregon at age 71' 1.22, 'born in Monterrey, Mexico on 12 May' 1.11, 'met his wife in Dublin, Ireland at a wedding' 1.03), a 'for <people> with <condition>' description followed by a street address ('a hostel for teenagers with mental health problems at 41 Station Road' 1.59, 'a shelter for men with ... problems at 149 W.' 2.4), a coordinated group of test subjects ('tested in dogs and monkeys for heart toxicity' 1.08) or web pages ('cookies record your activity on our websites for marketing purposes' 1.80); a name pair, coordination or parenthetical in that closed PP multiplies strength 2-8x over a bare common noun ('died in the quiet house at age 71' 0.15, 'tested in the laboratory for' 0.24). It stays below ~0.4 when the same preposition comes straight after the verb or its direct object (so moving the adjunct before the place PP kills it: 'died at age 71 in Portland, Oregon' 0.41 on the later ' in'; 'tested for heart toxicity in dogs' 0.12), after a PP whose object is a bare common noun, on ordinary noun-modifying PP chains ('the Gulf of Mexico', 'the shore of the lake', 'through the sealed port under', all < 0.2), after verbs like 'looked at', and when the closed name ends the sentence ('He moved to Denver, Colorado.' 0.14); ' in <year>' after a name pair is weaker (0.2-0.8) than ' at'/' on'.

Fires on a short subword fragment (typically a 2-4 character stem such as ' Fle', ' Ham', ' Mer', ' Trem', ' tre', 'ah', 'az', '.T', 'ED', or the first digit of a ZIP code) at the moment the text has started spelling out an unfamiliar surname, identifier, foreign all-caps word or code/number string that this token does not complete, so the model must still supply the rest of the unit; it is near-silent when the same characters form a complete familiar word or entity (' Ham' in 'West Ham', Danish ' tre', single-token names such as ' Smith', ' Hanks', ' Fleming') and much weaker on a later repeat of a name already spelled earlier in the context. Retrospective: its output uniformly promotes 'edge' tokens regardless of context and ablation changes the next-token distribution very little (KL ~0.005 at peaks), so it is not preparing the continuation.

Fires at the seam where an element of an already-established repeated text format ends and the next slot of that format begins — the import slot after a Java package header, later entries of a JSON/INI/SQL/email-header/comment/diff/citation/table/numbered-list block — and, in prose, at the quote-close+attribution or the comma/dash that closes a long parenthetical insertion whose embedded clause has a lexical verb and its complement. The trigger is the structural boundary rather than the surface token: the same `import`, `,"`, comma or newline in free prose, as a lone or first occurrence, or after a short or verbless/copular quotation stays below threshold.

Fires on a token (often the first subword of a word or name) that already occurred earlier in the same document, typically 30-500 tokens back, and now comes back in a new local context, i.e. the token(s) right before it were not followed by it at the earlier occurrence (e.g. 'earn a high ... earn the [[high]]', 'icosahedral nucleocapsid ... viral [[nucle]]ic', 'BackgroundColor="tomato" ... ForegroundColor="[[tom]]ato"'). It stays near zero on first mentions, gives only weak activation (about 0.1-0.3 of max) on tokens new to the document, and stays near zero when the token continues a verbatim copy of an earlier phrase (an induction-style exact repeat); long repetitive documents such as tables, choruses and repeated code lines give the largest values.

N2268- fires on the second token of a two-token unit that the preceding token has already committed to: a particle or preposition after an event/action word ('go about' 2.4, 'go over' 1.4, 'go around' 1.3, 'set up' 1.0, 'ready up' 1.1, 'plan up' 0.9, 'look about' 0.8), or the tail fragment of a word continued across two tokens ('Ke|isha' 1.1, 'Comp|iling' 0.7, 'Ans|ar' 0.6). Both tokens are required: the same particle after a determiner, pronoun or concrete noun is silent ('the up', 'hands up', 'table up', 'the word about' all ~0), the same verb with a particle outside the preferred set is near silent ('go back' 0.00, 'set out' 0.00, 'set aside' 0.00), and a non-event verb roughly quarters it ('put up' 0.37 vs 'set up' 1.16).

Fires on the final token that completes a multi-token proper name (software/framework, product, organisation, league, place) when that name is the topic label of a heading-like slot: the opening words of a title (e.g. a StackExchange 'Q:\n\n' title, a tournament/page title), an item in a 'Category:' list at the end of a wiki article, or a name the document has already established as its recurring subject. The same name inside ordinary running prose on first mention, a name broken by a function word, or a plain common noun stays near zero (< 0.2).

Fires in Java, Kotlin and Swift source on the token just before a type is written: a method or constructor name before its '(' parameter list (main, Notebook, getFromCache: 9-17), ',' between parameters, a field modifier ('private'/'public'/'final') in a field list, a Kotlin/Swift ':' or '->' before a type, or 'catch (', and in JavaScript at ' =', ' +', 'return' or '.floor' next to a 'Math.' call. It is strongest (9-17) when the expected type is a capitalised builtin such as String, Integer or Object and weaker (3-7) for int/boolean or user-defined classes, and it stays below ~3 in Python, TypeScript, Rust and C#-style lowercase 'string'/'str' code, in statement bodies with no declaration or Math call (loops, println, plain assignments or calls such as 'const totalPrice = CalculateDiscount(cartItems);'), and in ordinary prose, including person names.

This pole detects formulaic, stored text rather than composed prose: it peaks on the token where a memorized or repeated formula is recognised - the opening tokens of successive items of a packed QA/math-dataset list ('What is the greatest common divisor of', 'Calculate', 'Is', 'Does'), the attribution line of a licence/copyright header ('...and contributors.', 'The Chromium Authors'), and a small set of stock web strings ('We use cookies', 'You can unsubscribe at any time', 'Please enter your...'). It stays inactive for the same words in ordinary sentences and one-off questions, and for generic boilerplate that lacks those exact formulas ('All rights reserved', 'Powered by WordPress').

Fires on the non-final digits of a large numeral written with a thousands separator in running prose (prices, populations, square footage, viewer counts), peaking on the 1st and 2nd digit after the ',' (any digit value, not just '0'; weaker with '.'), and staying near zero on the last digit of a group, on spelled-out numbers ('seven thousand', '$25 million'), and on years and other short numbers.
